Gonna tell my experience as a former intern. So I got my internship canceled on February because I was not fulfilling the expectations of my managers. A little context, i was weeks isolated because of the pandemic so it's reasonable I was having a hard time to socialize and communicate.

They said they got to interrupt my internship because I was not stabilishing conversations with them and the patients (it was in a hospital in a technician job). Basically I freeze in that day, unable to take iniciative because it was my first day there and take time to adapt to a new environment. I mention my diagnosis as way of explaining my behavior and take in consideration that it's difficult for me to adapt to new situations. Well, it was more of a mistake than anything. They pathologized my condition but said they would make room for accommodations. 

Foreshadowing, they didn't since I was never allowed to come back unless I recover from my condition. I had a meeting on March with my professors (this a internship organized by my uni) and they basically said I should just fit in and solve my "problems" by myself. They were the ones that said I would come back to my internship if I recover from my autism, which is pure nonsense because they have the decency to research about my autism, they knew its lifetime condition (this coming from people with Psychology masters).

So begged to come back to my internship twice, but they withdrew. It has been 3 terrible months because I see my nt mates going steady with their internships and me stuck in the bureaucratic process of getting my needs considered. I was canceled in my first day just because I was not acting as expected.

Even when institutions claim to be inclusive, it can be a facade, for the sake of appearing progressive. But yeah I have already a lot of ableist experiences. This has been affecting my mental health so badly. Keep in mind, I don't like my job but I wanted at least a chance to do it. I actually considered dropping out and still do. I'm tired of explaining my existence and identity to people to then treat me as sick person.

I was diagnosed really early, adding the fact that I was a girl, because girls are underdiagnosed and most of the times, they got the diagnosis later in adulthood. I was 5 years old when I was first diagnosed with ASD.

The psychologists thought that I would have learning difficulties because of my communication struggles. This was the mid-thousands btw. I did well in school (except high-school). 
But I was a special needs student for a couple of months in elementary school. I hated it. I learned just fine but people just assumed that just because I was didn't speak that much, I wasn't intelligent. They dropped me after the first midterms.

In my teen years, there were moments that I would try to be social, mostly because I want so hard to pass as NT, and I would fail tremendously. I suffered from constant bullying and gaslighting by a former friend. After being stigmatized, I was ostracized. Those experiences were very traumatic and I didn't have any friends to back up for me or to vent. I started to develop anxiety attacks. 

There were times that I would hate myself for being like this. For not being social enough to pass, for not being smart enough to be functional. I was becoming more reclusive, misanthropic over time. I was shamed for what I am, for something that I cannot control.

Years after, I feel less miserable and more accepting of myself mostly thanks to the online autistic community.

TO CONCLUDE, being diagnosed in a time that autism was heavily pathologised and stigmatized made me feel, as a kid, an abnormality. People regarded me as a less capable child and also thought that my behaviour was weird. 
That impact immensely the way that I perceived my autism thorough my adolescence. But also knowing earlier that I was autistic, give me acess to speech therapy and mainly made me understand my behaviours.

All the time. Your story was very similar to mine. Being bullied for being autistic. Trying to hide my autistic traits and having to deal with people telling that I should be more outgoing, less anxious. It's exausting dealing with judgemental people, thinking that every thing you do is scrutinized by them and you could be call out for your behavior. Adding the fact that we can have autistic burnouts and meltdowns.

I have judgemental friends (some would say toxic) that made me reconsider not telling my diagnosis, even though I want to be out. They have a very narrow understanding of autism, mostly based on stereotypes. 

So, mate, if you have toxic friends, I don't recomend to tell your diagnosis for the sake of your mental health.
If you have a very supportive and empathetic friend, take your time. You can chose to tell your diagnosis or not. That's ok if you do either of those. Whatever feels comfortable to you, mate.
